description: Conformance vectors for the hashid ID format. Each group is a table test for one capability; each vector names the specification rules it pins. A vector carries either `expect` or `error`. Integers that do not fit a JSON double - u64 values and nanosecond timestamps - are carried as decimal strings.

conventions.error: the error code from hashid-spec.md section 15
conventions.reason: for a Malformed error, the grammar rule that broke
conventions.witness_and_near_miss: Where a rule draws a line, vectors come in pairs: a witness the rule must accept and a near-miss differing in one salient dimension that it must reject. The `note` says which is which.
conventions.store: `"store": "failing"` replaces the vector's id list with a store whose every lookup fails, to check that the failure is propagated rather than read as a negative answer.
conventions.expect_and_error: Every vector carries exactly one of `expect` (the value the operation must produce, which may be null where 'no value' is a real outcome) or `error` (the code from hashid-spec.md section 15). No group uses any other shape.

uncovered_rules.ES-4: Reaching the desperate nonce needs a store holding thousands of specific candidates; listing them would be most of this file, to pin one branch.
uncovered_rules.ES-5: Exhaustion needs the same store as ES-4.
uncovered_rules.SM-3: Needs a saturated slugged namespace, for the same reason.
uncovered_rules.ST-1: An obligation on the caller's store, not on the implementation's output: a static file cannot assert that your database answers. What IS checked is that the implementation propagates a failure rather than reading it as a negative answer - see ES-7 and RS-7.
uncovered_rules.ST-2: As ST-1: a fragment search is something the caller's store performs, so there is no output of this implementation for a vector to compare against. The rule it must satisfy, FM-1 to FM-4, is pinned by the `matches_fragment` group.
uncovered_rules.ST-3: As ST-1: whether a store CAN report failure is a property of the interface a binding exposes, not of a value. The `binding-guide.md` conformance checklist is where this one is checked, by a human.
uncovered_rules.ST-4: As ST-1: rejecting a malformed id returned by the caller's store needs a store that returns one, which a vector file has no way to supply.

base36.note: Zero is one character, not an empty string.
The alphabet starts at the digits.
Thirty-five is the last single digit.
Near-miss for B36-004: thirty-six rolls over.
Near-miss for B36-006: the first three-digit value.
The whole u64 range must encode. Values are strings because JSON numbers cannot carry 2^64-1.

seed.note: Absent optionals are encoded as `0:`, never omitted.
An empty title still carries its length prefix.
Witness for unforgeable boundaries: title 'a', description 'b'.
Near-miss for SEED-004: title 'a|b' with no description must NOT seed the same. This pair is the entire reason for the length prefix.
Lengths count BYTES, not characters: 'héllo wörld' is 11 characters and 13 bytes.
The nonce is last and decimal.
The Unix epoch is timestamp 0, which is a real value and not the out-of-range fallback.
A negative instant renders with its sign.

digest.note: One character: the tail of the encoding.
Four characters. Note DIG-002 is a suffix of this: truncation is from the tail.
Twelve characters, the collision fallback width.
Twenty characters: a u64 is at most 13 base36 digits, so this must LEFT-pad with zeros.
Thirteen characters is the full unpadded encoding of the leading u64.
Five characters of the same input: the tail of DIG-010.
A real seed string, hashed. This is what a mint actually digests: it is SEED-001's output, and MINT-011 mints the same content, so the three groups pin one chain end to end.
Near-miss: zero is not a length. There is no hash of zero characters.
Near-miss for DIG-014: one past the grammar's hash limit.

hash_length.note: Zero population takes the minimum. The zero case.
A hundred still fits three characters.
Witness for the 3-to-4 boundary at the default 0.25 bound.
Near-miss for LEN-004: one more record and four characters no longer stay under the bound.
A million saturates the default maximum.
Past saturation the answer does not grow.
A raised floor is honoured even when a shorter hash would do.
A lowered ceiling caps the answer, per LN-3.
A stricter bound widens sooner than LEN-006 does.

mint_unchecked.note: A different nonce is a different ID.
Eight characters. Its tail is MINT-001's hash.
The prefix does not perturb the hash: 'dtv' is the three-character tail of MINT-004.
An empty title is content too.
A prefix containing hyphens round-trips through the grammar.
Closes the chain: this request seeds to SEED-001's string, which digests to DIG-012's hash, which appears here as the minted ID.

parse_id.note: The split is at the LAST hyphen, so the prefix keeps its own.
Leading zeros in a child segment parse and canonicalize away.
Witness for the segment ceiling: the largest u32.
Near-miss for PARSE-008: one past the largest u32.
Witness for the length bounds: a 64-byte prefix and a 40-byte hash.
An ID longer than 105 bytes is legal when its parts are: the total is not separately enforced.
An uppercase prefix is rejected too.
A trailing dot leaves an empty segment.
A space is outside the prefix charset.
Every punctuation character the prefix allows.

format_id.note: An illegal prefix is refused rather than rendered.

normalize_prefix.note: Trim, lowercase, drop, and strip trailing punctuation.
A trailing separator would otherwise produce a doubled hyphen in the ID.
Near-miss: nothing usable survives, and no default is invented.
Punctuation only: kept by the charset, then stripped as trailing, leaving nothing.

parse_prefix.note: Near-miss for PPFX-001: uppercase is REJECTED here, where normalize would fold it.
The empty string is not a prefix.

abbreviate_prefix.note: Six bytes or fewer is unchanged.
Near-miss for ABBR-002: seven bytes, single word, first three alphanumerics.

normalize_slug.note: Spaces and punctuation collapse to single hyphens.
Runs collapse; each run yields exactly one hyphen.
A leading run produces nothing, because the output is still empty.
Truncation that lands on a hyphen re-trims it.
Nothing usable is 'no slug', not an error and not an empty slug.

join_prefix_slug.note: The slug is normalized on the way in.
An unusable slug yields no composite prefix.
The slug is truncated to the remaining budget: 64 - (2 + 1) = 61.
A 64-byte prefix leaves a budget below zero, so nothing fits.
Witness for the budget edge: a 62-byte prefix leaves room for exactly one character.
Near-miss for JOIN-006: a 63-byte prefix leaves a budget of zero.

id_parent.note: Two levels: only the last segment is removed.
A root has no parent. Not an error.

id_child.note: Zero is a legal child index.

id_depth.note: A root is depth zero. The zero case.

is_descendant_of.note: Near-miss: an ID is never a descendant of itself.
Near-miss: a sibling branch does not descend.
A different hash is a different tree.
A different prefix is a different tree.
The ancestor cannot be deeper than the descendant.

matches_fragment.note: A fragment matches anywhere in the hash, not only at the start.
With no child part in the fragment, the ID's child path is ignored.
Witness: the child path matches exactly.
Near-miss for FRG-006: the parent must NOT match a fragment that names a child.
Near-miss for FRG-006: a sibling must not match either.
Near-miss for FRG-006: a deeper descendant is not an exact child-path match.
The empty fragment is a substring of every hash.

validate_prefix.note: Near-miss: a different prefix, with no allow-list.
The allow-list admits an imported namespace.
An allow-list that does not include it.

mint.note: Nothing taken: nonce 0 wins, and the result equals MINT-001.
Nonce 0 is taken, so the ladder steps to nonce 1 (MINT-002) rather than return a known-taken ID.
The first eight nonces are taken; nonce 8 wins.
Nine taken; the last nonce of the first rung wins.
All ten three-character candidates are taken, so the hash WIDENS by one and restarts at nonce 0.
Widened, and the first widened candidate is taken too.
With max_hash_length pinned to the minimum, exhausting the first rung drops straight to the twelve-character fallback.
The store cannot answer. Minting propagates that rather than treating it as 'not taken' — which would invent an ID that may already exist.

mint_with_slug.note: The slug is folded into the prefix and the hash is still appended. The hash equals MINT-001's, since the prefix does not perturb it.
An unusable slug falls back to a plain mint.
A slug that cannot fit the prefix budget falls back to a plain mint.
The slugged ladder steps nonces exactly as the plain one does.

resolve.note: Trimmed and lowercased first, and the input is echoed back verbatim.
A bare hash gets the default prefix.
A unique fragment of a hash.
A fragment from the middle of a hash.
A hyphen pins the namespace: 'br-ab' searches for 'ab' within 'br'.
Near-miss for RES-006: the same fragment pinned to the other namespace.
Ambiguity names every candidate, sorted, so a caller can present a choice.
Witness with substring matching off: a complete hash still resolves.
Near-miss for RES-012: a fragment does not, with substring matching off.
An exact match wins over a substring one: 'br-abc' is itself a known ID here.
A bare hash CARRYING a child path still takes the default-prefix step, because prepending the prefix yields a complete existing ID. RS-4 is tried before RS-5.
Near-miss for RES-015: '4up6.4' is a fragment, so the default-prefix step forms 'br-4up6.4', which does not exist, and resolution falls through to a substring match whose child path must be exact.
The store cannot answer. Resolution reports a store failure, NOT 'not found': a caller that deletes on 'not found' needs the difference.

config_validation.note: Witness for the lower bound: min may equal max.
Near-miss for CFG-002: zero is not a length.
An inverted range is not satisfiable.
Near-miss for CFG-005: one past the grammar's hash limit.
Near-miss: zero is not a probability, and a bound of zero is unreachable.
Near-miss: certainty is not a bound either.
